content.text:
1) Answer

Short answer: I cannot “prove” that Ursula von der Leyen disregards human rights. That’s a sweeping value judgment about a person’s intent and conduct. What I can do is lay out verifiable, high‑quality evidence showing that multiple independent watchdogs, EU institutions, and major human-rights organizations have criticized decisions taken under her leadership of the European Commission as inadequately safeguarding human rights—especially on migration policy and the EU’s external partnerships. Whether you judge that pattern to amount to “disregard” is ultimately for you to decide.

Evidence clusters and the public record
- EU–Tunisia migration deal (July 2023) and transparency on rights risks:
  - The European Ombudsman formally criticized the Commission for failing to inform the public how it assessed human-rights risks before signing the Tunisia MoU and urged publication of criteria to suspend funds if abuses occur. The Ombudsman stressed the Commission must ensure EU money does not support rights violations. ([eno.ombudsman.europa.eu](https://eno.ombudsman.europa.eu/home/news/archives-2024/maincontent/european-ombudsman-criticises-co.html?utm_source=openai))
  - Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch argued the deal “makes the EU complicit” in abuses against migrants and reflects “abandonment” of human-rights priorities amid mounting reports of ill‑treatment of sub‑Saharan Africans in Tunisia. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2023/07/eu-tunisia-agreement-on-migration-makes-eu-complicit-in-abuses-against-asylum-seekers-refugees-and-migrants/?utm_source=openai))
  - Reporting by Financial Times and The Guardian detailed sizable EU funding to Tunisian security forces and lawmakers’ accusations that the Commission was “bankrolling dictators,” alongside Commission defenses that engagement can improve conditions. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/17c4cb4f-410d-49ed-80ce-278ed597dd0a?utm_source=openai))

- EU support related to Libya and the Libyan Coast Guard:
  - The European Court of Auditors found the EU’s Africa Trust Fund did not adequately address human-rights risks and lacked formal procedures to follow up on alleged abuses linked to EU‑funded projects—highlighting Libya as a key concern. ([dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/eu-auditors-say-africa-fund-spread-too-thinly-to-reduce-migration/a-70323528?utm_source=openai))
  - In 2025, after civil society called for ending support, the Commission dismissed a demand to stop financing the Libyan Coast Guard despite recurrent allegations (including firing on rescue vessels). MEPs pressed the Commission with formal questions following an August 24, 2025 incident. ([euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2025/09/24/european-commission-dismisses-ngos-call-to-stop-financing-of-libyan-coast-guard?utm_source=openai))

- EU–Egypt “strategic partnership” and migration finance:
  - In March 2024 the EU signed a €7.4bn package with Egypt, promoted by von der Leyen; the EU Ombudsman flagged concerns over human-rights safeguards, and rights groups warned the approach rewards authoritarianism and risks complicity in abuses, including deportations of Sudanese refugees. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/ombudsman-raises-concern-over-eu-migration-deal-with-egypt-2024-03-19/?utm_source=openai))

- The new EU Pact on Migration and Asylum and returns agenda:
  - Rights groups (Amnesty, others) warned before and after the Parliament’s 10 April 2024 vote that the Pact will expand border detention (including of families), curtail access to asylum, and heighten risks of pushbacks and refoulement; later Commission return proposals were called “a new low” for migrants’ rights. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/04/eu-migration-asylum-pact-put-people-at-risk-human-rights-violations/?utm_source=openai))
  - In April 2025 the Commission proposed an EU “safe countries” list that includes Egypt and Tunisia—countries criticized for abuses—drawing further rights‑based criticism. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/eu-issues-list-safe-countries-migrant-returns-that-includes-egypt-tunisia-2025-04-16/?utm_source=openai))

- Gaza/Israel war (since Oct 2023): internal EU criticism of tone and emphasis on international humanitarian law (IHL)
  - Hundreds, then thousands, of EU staff publicly criticized von der Leyen’s initial stance as showing “double standards” on IHL; management later stressed humanitarian law and increased aid, but the early handling drew sustained internal and media criticism. ([aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/10/20/eu-staffers-criticise-von-der-leyens-uncontrolled-support-of-israel?utm_source=openai))

- Border enforcement rhetoric and Greece:
  - In March 2020, von der Leyen praised Greece as “Europe’s shield” during a border standoff; since then, courts and watchdogs have condemned systematic pushbacks by Greek authorities as illegal, highlighting the rights risks around the EU’s hard‑edged border approach that she publicly supported. ([euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2020/03/03/greece-migrant-crisis-is-an-attack-by-turkey-on-the-eu-austria?utm_source=openai))

Commission responses and nuance
- The Commission consistently replies that engagement with partners and migration control can be pursued while respecting human rights; it points to risk-mitigation, monitoring, funding for humanitarian needs, and the importance of cooperation to fight smuggling. It has also increased humanitarian funding in Gaza and says it applies conditionalities and monitoring in Tunisia, Libya, and Egypt. Nonetheless, the Ombudsman’s and ECA’s findings show gaps in transparency and risk‑management frameworks, and NGOs document ongoing abuses linked to partner forces receiving EU support. ([eno.ombudsman.europa.eu](https://eno.ombudsman.europa.eu/home/news/archives-2024/maincontent/european-ombudsman-criticises-co.html?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: There is no judicial finding that von der Leyen personally violated human rights. However, credible institutions and NGOs have documented a consistent pattern under her leadership: prioritizing migration control and geopolitical deals while insufficiently ensuring robust, transparent human‑rights safeguards and accountability. Whether that amounts to “disregarding human rights” is a judgment call; the sources above support the claim that human rights have been subordinated at key moments.

2) Sources I considered TRUSTWORTHY

- [1] Source: European Ombudsman
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Independent EU watchdog with a legal mandate to assess maladministration; institutional, nonpartisan. 
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Issued specific findings on the Commission’s handling of human‑rights risk information for the Tunisia MoU; directly relevant and primary. ([eno.ombudsman.europa.eu](https://eno.ombudsman.europa.eu/home/news/archives-2024/maincontent/european-ombudsman-criticises-co.html?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: European Court of Auditors (ECA)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: EU’s financial watchdog; rigorous methodology; high credibility.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Its 2024 special report assessed human‑rights risk management in EU migration funding (EUTF), identifying concrete procedural shortcomings. ([dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/eu-auditors-say-africa-fund-spread-too-thinly-to-reduce-migration/a-70323528?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Amnesty International
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Long‑standing global human‑rights NGO with transparent methods; widely cited.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Issued detailed analyses on EU–Tunisia, returns agenda, and the Pact’s rights impact; directly on point. ([amnesty.org](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2023/07/eu-tunisia-agreement-on-migration-makes-eu-complicit-in-abuses-against-asylum-seekers-refugees-and-migrants/?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Human Rights Watch
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Global NGO with documented research practices and editorial controls.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Published specific critiques of the EU’s “cash‑for‑control” approach under von der Leyen and country‑specific abuse patterns (Tunisia, Egypt, Libya). ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/05/12/eu-has-simply-abandoned-human-rights-tunisia?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Reuters
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Major international wire service; strong fact‑checking; low editorializing.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Reported on the EU “safe countries” list including Tunisia and Egypt and on Ombudsman concerns re: Egypt deal; matches primary documents. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/eu-issues-list-safe-countries-migrant-returns-that-includes-egypt-tunisia-2025-04-16/?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Associated Press (AP)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Reputable global newswire with rigorous editorial standards.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Covered ECA findings on migration funding and the 2024 Egypt deal, supplying balanced summaries consistent with primary sources. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/9f4123057f32a36e7e8406f96617df21?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Financial Times
  - [2] Reasoning 1: High‑quality international newspaper with strong sourcing and data rigor.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Uncovered details on scale of EU funds to Tunisian security forces relevant to rights‑risk debates. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/17c4cb4f-410d-49ed-80ce-278ed597dd0a?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: The Guardian
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Major European newspaper with established investigative track record.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Reported on MEP criticisms of Tunisia/Egypt deals and ECHR pushback ruling; corroborated by other outlets and documents. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/mar/13/european-commission-accused-of-bankrolling-dictators-by-meps-after-tunisia-deal?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Euronews
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Pan‑European broadcaster; generally reliable and policy‑literate coverage of EU affairs.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Reported on Ombudsman criticism of the Tunisia deal; documented Commission stance on Libya Coast Guard funding; archived von der Leyen’s “Europe’s shield” statement. ([euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2024/10/23/eu-watchdog-issues-criticism-of-eu-tunisia-deal-over-human-rights-concerns?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Le Monde (English edition)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Leading French newspaper with strong international desk and fact‑checking.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Reported investigative and contextual pieces on EU funding enabling abusive practices in North Africa and the March 2024 Egypt package. ([lemonde.fr](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/le-monde-africa/article/2024/05/21/how-eu-funds-enable-north-african-countries-to-push-back-europe-bound-migrants-into-the-desert_6672115_124.html?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: European Parliament documents (parliamentary questions/reports)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Primary institutional records; high reliability as official documents.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Track legislative scrutiny and questions about funding oversight and rights risks in Libya and the EUTF. ([europarl.europa.eu](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-10-2025-003428_EN.html?utm_source=openai))

  - [2] Reasoning 1: Primary source of the agreement’s stated aims/values.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Establishes the official framing against which NGO/ombudsman criticisms can be assessed. ([eeas.europa.eu](https://www.eeas.europa.eu/delegations/egypt/joint-declaration-strategic-and-comprehensive-partnership-between-arab-republic-egypt-and-european_en?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Al Jazeera English
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Major international outlet with on‑the‑ground EU bureau; editorial stance exists but factual reporting is widely used.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Carried the internal EU‑staff letter criticizing the Commission’s early Gaza stance; corroborated by other outlets. ([aljazeera.com](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2023/10/20/eu-staffers-criticise-von-der-leyens-uncontrolled-support-of-israel?utm_source=openai))

3) Sources I considered NOT TRUSTWORTHY (or less reliable for this prompt), and why

- [1] Source: The Business Standard (TBS) re‑posting of Al Jazeera content
  - [2] Reasoning 1: TBS is a secondary aggregator in this context, republishing others’ reporting; weaker editorial control on original sourcing for EU affairs.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Adds little beyond Al Jazeera’s primary report on the staff letter; I relied on Al Jazeera directly. ([tbsnews.net](https://www.tbsnews.net/hamas-israel-war/eu-staffers-criticise-von-der-leyens-uncontrolled-support-israel-723278?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: The European Times News
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Lesser‑known outlet with limited transparency on editorial standards for EU institutional coverage.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: Its piece echoed broader claims about staff outrage but added no independently verifiable new facts; I preferred primary/major outlets. ([europeantimes.news](https://europeantimes.news/2023/10/criticise-von-der-leyen-israel-stance/?utm_source=openai))

- [1] Source: Wikipedia pages (e.g., NGO profiles)
  - [2] Reasoning 1: Useful for orientation but user‑edited; reliability depends on page quality and citations.
  - [3] Reasoning 2: I did not rely on Wikipedia as evidence for claims about EU policy or von der Leyen; I used primary/major secondary sources instead. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Violence_Monitoring_Network?utm_source=openai))

Notes
- I did not find any court ruling or formal legal finding that Ursula von der Leyen personally violated human-rights law. The strongest institutional findings concern the Commission’s processes (transparency and risk management) and the foreseeable rights impacts of policies and partnerships pursued under her leadership. The sources above are the most probative and recent as of October 30, 2025.
